title: SYSK Selects: How Jackhammers Work
summary: A rerun Selects episode of Stuff You Should Know, originally released in February 2016, in which the hosts examine the jackhammer: its origins in mining and tunneling, the pneumatic design pioneered by Charles Brady King and others, how the trigger valve and piston drive the chisel bit, why compressed air suits mines, the cracking mechanics of concrete breaking, and health and safety hazards including noise, silica dust, hand-arm vibration, and vibration sickness. Also covers an electric and a helium-based quieter jackhammer prototype, New York City jackhammer noise complaints, and a listener mail shout-out for the Totally Cool, Totally Art program in Austin, Texas.

segments.title: Rerun intro and knife gift shout-out
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the rerun of the infamous jackhammer episode, then the hosts thank listeners for a handmade filet and chef's knife from built Sharp Knives and banter about knives and noise of leaf blowers versus jackhammers.

segments.title: Jackhammer basics and history of hand tools
segments.summary: The hosts describe the jackhammer as a hardcore hammer and chisel that removes the human from each strike, contrast it with sledgehammers and pick axes used in mining, and note the physical toll of operating a roughly hundred-pound tool.

segments.title: Origins: Sardinia tunnel and early percussion drills
segments.summary: The hosts recount a twelve-kilometer mountain train tunnel in Sardinia around 1840 that spurred early pneumatic tool development, including Jonathan Couch's 1848 percussion drill and Joseph Foul's use of air power in the 1850s.

segments.title: Charles Brady King and pneumatic design
segments.summary: Charles Brady King is credited with the handheld pneumatic jackhammer and holding its patent; the hosts digress into his automotive work in Detroit before explaining why air power suits mining, where combustion engines and sparks are hazardous.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A brief break in the episode before returning to the content.

segments.title: Electric versus pneumatic and inner workings
segments.summary: The hosts compare small electric hardware-store jackhammers with large pneumatic ones, explain the weight role, and describe the piston, trigger valve, and spring that drive the chisel bit up and down, plus the cattle-stunning pneumatic analogy and hydraulic jackhammers.

segments.title: How concrete breaks and bit selection
segments.summary: The hosts explain that jackhammering first pulverizes concrete into a crushed zone that transmits force and creates cracks that propagate until chunks break off, and that bit shape affects cracking and removal of debris.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A brief break in the episode before the health and safety discussion.

segments.title: Jackhammer safety and health hazards
segments.summary: The hosts discuss bits getting stuck, sharp bits, noise levels near a jet engine, silica dust causing lung cancer risk and water spraying, hand-arm vibration and Raynaud's phenomenon, whole-body vibration, vibration sickness, and basic protective gear and utility line marking.

segments.title: Quieter jackhammer prototypes and NYC noise
segments.summary: The hosts describe a Brookhaven National Laboratory helium-powered Raptor jackhammer with about 87 decibels and a 2011 electric model at about 100 decibels, the construction industry's resistance to them, and New York City noise complaints about jackhammering.

segments.title: Listener mail: Totally Cool, Totally Art
segments.summary: A listener from Austin, Texas, Brian Friedtog, describes the free after-school arts program Totally Cool, Totally Art and asks for a shout-out; the hosts mention a possible South by Southwest appearance.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give contact information and sign off.
